title: GZIP file format specification version 4.3
summary: Defines the gzip file format, a lossless compressed data format compatible with the widely used gzip utility. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC defines how gzip files store compressed data so different programs can read and write the same format. Each member includes information that helps identify the format and check the uncompressed data.

questions: what is the gzip file format
how does the gzip header work
what are the gzip magic bytes
subtitle: The gzip file format: a sequence of members with headers, compressed data and integrity checks.

tldr.problem: Software needs a portable compressed-data format that can process streams using bounded intermediate storage and detect data corruption.
tldr.mechanism: A gzip file contains one or more members. Each member has a header, compressed blocks and a trailer containing CRC32 and the uncompressed size modulo 2^32.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1952 is an Informational specification that documents the gzip file format and its compliance rules.

today: RFC 1952 is an Informational RFC that specifies the gzip file format. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Goals and Scope of the Format
sections.content:
RFC 1952 defines a lossless compressed-data format independent of CPU type, operating system, file system and character set. It is intended for stream compression and decompression using a bounded amount of intermediate storage and is compatible with files produced by the gzip utility.

The format uses DEFLATE as its compression method in this specification and can be extended to other methods. It does not provide random access to compressed data or aim to outperform specialized compression methods on specialized data.
sections.plainLanguage: The format lets programs compress and decompress data streams in a portable way. It does not define random access to a compressed file.

sections.title: Members and the Fixed Header
sections.content:
A gzip file is a series of members placed one after another. Each member begins with a fixed 10-byte header containing identification bytes, a compression method, flags, a modification time, extra flags and an operating-system value. The identification bytes are 31 (0x1f) and 139 (0x8b); method 8 denotes DEFLATE.

Multi-byte numbers are stored with the least-significant byte first. Header flags can indicate extra data, an original file name, a human-readable comment or a header CRC. The modification time uses Unix format, and zero means no timestamp is available.
sections.plainLanguage: Each member starts with a fixed header that identifies gzip and describes the compression method. Flags show whether optional information follows the header.

sections.title: Optional Header Fields
sections.content:
The header can include an extra field, the original file name, a comment and a CRC16 of the header. The extra field contains subfields, each with an identifier and a length. Names and comments use ISO 8859-1 (Latin-1) characters and end with a zero byte.

Reserved flag bits must be zero. The extra field can hold application-specific information; this RFC identifies Apollo file-type information as one defined subfield.
sections.plainLanguage: Optional header fields can preserve a file name, a comment or extra information. A reader checks the flags to know which fields to skip or process.

sections.title: Compressed Blocks and the Trailer
sections.content:
After the header and any optional fields come the compressed blocks. Each member ends with an 8-byte trailer: CRC32 checks the uncompressed data, and ISIZE records the input size modulo 2^32.

The RFC requires a compliant compressor to produce correct identification bytes, method, CRC32 and ISIZE. A compliant decompressor checks the identification bytes and method, can skip optional header fields, and reports an error if a reserved flag is non-zero.
sections.plainLanguage: The trailer contains a check value for the original data and its size modulo 2^32. A decompressor checks key header fields and reports invalid reserved bits.

sections.title: Checking Data Integrity
sections.content:
Compression removes redundancy, so corruption in compressed data can have severe effects and may be difficult to correct. The RFC recommends that systems using gzip provide a way to validate data integrity.

The format includes a CRC32 check value for uncompressed data, which a decompressor can recalculate and compare with the trailer.
sections.plainLanguage: Corruption in compressed data can make the result difficult to recover. The RFC recommends checking the CRC32 value to detect damage.
